Empty
ĕmp´ty
adj. and v. (containing nothing, void; rendering Hebrew req, reyqam, Greek kenos)
From Anglo-Saxon aemtig, at leisure, unoccupied. Scripture uses emptiness both as a plight and as a promise — no one is to leave God's presence, or God's people's service, empty.

Biblical Definition

Empty is a word about hands. God's standing rule for worship is that no one comes with nothing: “none shall appear before me empty” (Exo 23:15; Exo 34:20). And His standing rule for release is that no one leaves with nothing: “when thou sendest him out free from thee, thou shalt not let him go away empty” (Deu 15:13). Even the exodus obeys it — “when ye go, ye shall not go empty” (Exo 3:21) — slaves leaving four centuries of unpaid labour with wages at last. Jacob measures Laban's injustice by the same word: but for God, “surely thou hadst sent me away now empty” (Gen 31:42). And the emptiest place in Genesis is the pit into which Joseph was cast: “the pit was empty, there was no water in it” (Gen 37:24) — a detail supplied so the reader knows he did not drown, and so the brothers could sit down to eat beside it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines empty as containing nothing, or nothing but air — and figuratively as destitute of solid matter, of sense, or of substance; vain; unsatisfactory.

expand to see more

EMP´TY, a. Containing nothing, or nothing but air; as an empty chest; empty space.

2. Devoid; destitute; as a mind empty of good.

3. Destitute of solid matter, of sense, of knowledge; as empty words; an empty coxcomb.

4. Unfurnished; unsupplied; as an empty house. 5. Void; vacant.

Key Scripture

Exo 23:15 — "Thou shalt keep the feast of unleavened bread: (thou shalt eat unleavened bread seven days, as I commanded thee, in the time appointed of the month Abib; for in it thou camest out from Egypt: and none shall appear before me empty:)"

Deu 15:13 — "And when thou sendest him out free from thee, thou shalt not let him go away empty:"

Exo 3:21 — "And I will give this people favour in the sight of the Egyptians: and it shall come to pass, that, when ye go, ye shall not go empty:"

Gen 37:24 — "And they took him, and cast him into a pit: and the pit was empty, there was no water in it."

Modern Corruption

Worship approached empty-handed as a matter of course, and workers released empty as a matter of contract — both against a law that requires the hands to be full in either direction.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The neglected law is symmetrical and worth restoring in both halves. Godward: none shall appear before me empty. The New Testament does not repeat the specific offerings, and it nowhere reverses the instinct — a worship in which nothing is brought, given, or offered has lost something the feasts of Israel took for granted. Manward: thou shalt not let him go away empty. A servant leaving in the seventh year was to be furnished liberally out of the flock, the floor, and the winepress, which is a standard of severance no employment contract requires and every Christian employer should feel.

The principle joining the two is that God fills empty hands and expects His people to do the same. Exodus 3:21 is the clearest case: a nation of slaves with four hundred years of unpaid labour behind them does not leave empty, and the wages come from the very people who withheld them. Genesis 37:24 supplies the counter-image of hardness — the pit was empty, and the brothers sat down to eat bread beside it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew req (H7386), empty, vain, worthless; reyqam (H7387), emptily, without cause; Greek kenos (G2756), empty, hollow — the root of the verb Paul uses of Christ emptying Himself.

expand to see more

Hebrew req (H7386) — empty, vain; the empty pit of Gen 37:24 and the empty ears of Pharaoh's dream (Gen 41:27).

Hebrew reyqam (H7387) — empty-handed, without cause; the standing word in none shall appear before me empty (Exo 23:15).

Greek kenoo (G2758) — to empty, make void; made himself of no reputation (Php 2:7) is literally emptied himself.

Usage

"“None shall appear before me empty” — hands full toward God."

"“Thou shalt not let him go away empty” — hands full toward the departing servant."

"“The pit was empty, there was no water in it” — and they sat down to eat bread."
